title: How Students Use AI Feedback Matters: Experimental Evidence on Physics Achievement and Autonomy
extended_summary:
The paper examines whether generative-AI-powered feedback helps high school physics students, and especially whether its effects depend on how students are required or allowed to use it. Rather than treating AI feedback as a single intervention, the study compares different usage patterns and asks how these patterns affect both academic achievement and learner autonomy/self-regulated learning across students with different baseline achievement levels.

The authors conducted two randomized controlled trials in one high school in southwest China. In Experiment 1, Grade 10 students were randomly assigned to compulsory personalized recommendation conditions: AI-generated heuristic solution hints plus workbook answers, workbook-based answers/explanations only, or no recommendation. In Experiment 2, students were randomly assigned to autonomous on-demand AI help with full student control, on-demand help with shared student-system control, or a control condition. Both experiments lasted five weeks and used paper-based workflows because smart devices were prohibited in classrooms.

The study found heterogeneous effects by achievement level and usage pattern. Under compulsory personalized recommendation, low-achieving students improved in physics achievement when receiving AI-generated heuristic hints, while high-achieving students showed declines in self-regulated learning without clear achievement gains. Under autonomous on-demand use, fully learner-controlled AI feedback improved achievement for high-achieving students without reducing autonomy, but lower-achieving students exposed to on-demand AI showed declines in autonomy, especially in dimensions overlapping with self-regulation.

The main conclusion is that the educational impact of GAI feedback depends strongly on both learner characteristics and usage pattern. The authors argue that AI feedback systems should not only optimize the precision of content but should also be designed around when, how, and by whom AI assistance is used, with different scaffolding strategies for students at different achievement levels.

identified_tools.name: Adaptive Feedback System (General)
identified_tools.description: An unnamed generative-AI-powered personalized feedback system that provides physics problem feedback, heuristic solution hints, concept explanations, and related practice recommendations through paper-based submission and retrieval/generation workflows.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied in two five-week randomized controlled trials with high school physics students: Experiment 1 tested compulsory personalized recommendations with GAI-generated heuristic solution hints, and Experiment 2 tested autonomous on-demand GAI feedback under full learner control or shared student-system control.

findings.finding_summary: In Experiment 1, compulsory use of personalized recommendations with GAI-generated heuristic solution hints significantly improved physics academic performance for low-achieving Grade 10 students relative to the control condition (d = 0.673, p < 0.05). The analyzed Experiment 1 sample was n = 121; the bottom-third subgroup included 13 students in the GAI-hints group and 10 in the control group, with 16 students in the workbook-recommendation comparison group.

In Experiment 1, high-achieving students experienced a significant decline in self-regulated learning under the compulsory personalized recommendation usage pattern, with no significant achievement gains reported (d = -0.477, p < 0.05). The analyzed Experiment 1 sample was n = 121; the top-third subgroup included 15 students in the GAI-hints group, 12 in the workbook-recommendation group, and 14 in the control group.

In Experiment 2, fully learner-controlled on-demand AI feedback significantly enhanced academic performance for high-achieving students (d = 0.378, p < 0.05). The paper reports that this achievement gain occurred without negatively impacting their autonomy.

In Experiment 2, autonomy declined among lower achievers exposed to on-demand AI interventions (d = -0.383, p < 0.05). The decline was especially notable in the technical-psychological dimension, which overlaps substantially with self-regulation (d = -0.549, p < 0.05).
findings.measure: learner autonomy questionnaire, including technical-psychological dimension

quality_tier_rationale: The paper reports two individually randomized controlled trials with baseline balance checks, control groups, covariate-adjusted regressions, and robust standard errors. Quality is downgraded from blue because of substantial attrition from recruited to analyzed samples and limited reporting of confidence intervals/subgroup sample sizes for several headline effects.
impact_tier_rationale: The RCTs report medium-to-large statistically significant subgroup effects in both positive and negative directions: achievement gains for low-achieving students under compulsory GAI hints and high-achieving students under learner-controlled on-demand help, but declines in SRL/autonomy for other groups. Because impacts are heterogeneous and include potential harms, the overall impact is mixed rather than uniformly positive.
